This game has incredibly good gameplay, and a decent story that allows them to play with the idea of pulling data from a bunch of different game genres with their own styles of cards. It's a lot of fun finding and exploiting new combos as you play. It's nothing like MMBN/OSFE, which is what I was expecting, but that's not the problem. The problem with the game is that it's aggressively anime in the ways that are pretty cringy and gross for the regular western audience. I can only hear "So this is what you like? I like that honest side of you" as a CG of an actual child pressing herself against you cuts in or "I'm a real adult now, no need to fret" from a busty teenager giving you bedroom eyes so many times before I just feel really gross. It's a shame because these things are tied to Muses, which are core parts of your comboing potential. I can tolerate a lot of the less palatable tropes found in anime, but this one I just couldn't. If the aggressive anime trappings don't bother you, by all means, the game is a very good deckbuilder. If they do though, you'll probably want to give it a pass.

I honestly played this game under the impression it was going to be Mega Man Battle Network. At the end of the day, it is not; it is its own game. To my surprise, it is not necessarily a bad thing. Not just in gameplay, but even in the story, everything has a unique aspect. Continuing on the comparison of Mega Man Battle Network, this is a smaller game; there is no sandbox world to explore. Instead, there are set levels with different themes that would also change your deck. Gameplay-wise, you have to manage the cards you have, not only for attacking but for movement. With the added challenge of not being able to bring your own personalized deck, you would have to learn what every card does. At first, I wasn't a fan of that, but once you find a deck you like, you are going to miss it. I have caught myself many times trying to sneak in those same cards that carried me. Overall, the gameplay has its charm; it gives you the feeling of popping off combos in Yu-Gi-Oh and destroying your opponent with your fourth-dimensional thinking. I'm going to avoid story spoilers, but I would try to summarize what you're doing. You go into video games and learn what the game is about. While you're learning about said game, you encounter the characters not only on the map but inside your decks, too. One of the coolest things about this game is that you will sometimes meet characters from previous games of Inti Creates, so if you're a fan of that company, you're going to see some recognizable characters. The lore behind these in-game video games is high-key interesting. I do hope some of these games actually become real. IDK man, they were cooking something with that one high school kid dating giant robot women. Y'all just ain't ready for it. Also, the way they debuted Divine Dynamo Flamefrit with this game was genius.

Someone said this is an Ipad game, some said this is nothing like a megaman game that was exclusive to the gameboy SP and for that reason you should ignore them. This is hands down a fun game. It's not like Slay the Spire where you play cards accordingly to your spending points system. So far each card has an SP value to play them, as well as allowing you to move up, down, left, right instead of playing the card and this adds a dynamic to the fighting mechanic. There's also mini bosses you defeat that are recruited and can be spawn by playing certain cards. Overall its a fun experience if you don't have someone ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ about an old game they once played. The story doesn't need to make 100% sense, its a damn FICTIONAL anime story and that says a lot. The characters are cute, the voice acting in english is literally what you would expect from an anime dub and the fighting mechanics are fun. That's it. If you only wanna play cards and use two neurons to figure out the best strategy than this is your kind of game. If you enjoy girls talking in anime voice pitch then ignore this game.

Card-en-Ciel is a unique fusion of roguelite progression, tactical card battles, and Japanese role-playing storytelling developed and published by INTI CREATES CO., LTD. Rather than following the familiar formula of traditional deckbuilding games, it introduces players to a virtual gaming universe where digital worlds collide and fictional characters become sentient. You step into the role of Neon, a detective who specializes in investigating incidents occurring inside virtual reality games. His latest case quickly evolves into an adventure filled with mysterious anomalies, colorful personalities, and countless references to fictional game worlds, creating a setting that feels imaginative and packed with charm from beginning to end. The game's strongest quality is its combat system, which combines strategic card management with movement across a battlefield grid. Every encounter requires players to think beyond simply playing the strongest card available, as positioning, enemy placement, and movement all influence the outcome of battles. This extra tactical layer makes combat feel more dynamic than many deckbuilders, rewarding thoughtful planning and clever combinations rather than relying solely on luck. Since each expedition features randomized encounters and evolving deck choices, every run encourages experimentation while maintaining a satisfying sense of unpredictability. An impressive feature is the enormous collection of more than 300 collectible cards, each representing a distinct character rather than a simple combat ability. Every character comes with voiced dialogue and unique interactions, giving the deck far more personality than expected. Instead of functioning as disposable resources, the cards become memorable companions that react to events and occasionally acknowledge one another during battle. This design helps establish a stronger emotional connection with the growing collection and makes discovering new cards consistently rewarding throughout the adventure. Card-en-Ciel also stands out through its presentation. The colorful anime-inspired artwork, expressive character illustrations, and energetic battle effects create an appealing visual style that complements its upbeat atmosphere. The soundtrack deserves special praise, particularly through the Muse system, which allows powerful support characters to trigger fully voiced musical performances during combat. Rather than serving as simple background music, these songs become part of the gameplay itself, transforming important moments into memorable audiovisual showcases. The variety of vocal tracks and musical styles helps each virtual world establish its own identity while adding excitement to longer play sessions. The story offers far more substance than is usually expected from a roguelite card game. Dialogue between characters is lively, humorous, and occasionally emotional, while the mystery surrounding the corrupted virtual worlds provides a compelling reason to continue progressing. Players familiar with INTI CREATES' previous works will appreciate numerous references and cameos, but newcomers can still enjoy the narrative because the characters are introduced naturally and remain entertaining regardless of prior knowledge. The balance between storytelling and gameplay keeps the pacing engaging without allowing either element to dominate the experience. While the game offers tremendous depth, it also asks players to invest time in learning its mechanics. The combination of deck construction, battlefield positioning, numerous card abilities, and layered combat systems creates a steeper learning curve than many games in the genre. New players may initially feel overwhelmed by the sheer number of strategic possibilities, and building effective decks requires patience and experimentation. Fortunately, once the mechanics become familiar, the complexity evolves into one of the game's greatest strengths rather than a barrier. Replay value is another major highlight. Randomized dungeon layouts, countless deck combinations, unlockable cards, and evolving strategies ensure that repeated runs remain enjoyable long after the main story concludes. Every playthrough presents fresh opportunities to discover new synergies, refine tactics, and overcome increasingly difficult encounters. This constant sense of progression keeps the gameplay rewarding while encouraging players to revisit earlier strategies with newly acquired cards and abilities. Card-en-Ciel succeeds because it refuses to settle for being just another deckbuilding roguelite. Its combination of tactical movement, engaging storytelling, memorable characters, excellent music, and extensive card collection creates an experience that feels both ambitious and polished. Although its complexity may discourage players looking for a more casual experience, those willing to learn its systems will find a rewarding adventure filled with creativity and impressive attention to detail. Rating: 8/10

Card-like roguelites are dime a dozen, but this one stands clear above the pack by virtue of its gamey aesthetic and amazing soundtrack. Not to mention that the game is so mechanically complex yet relatively simple to learn. You can genuinely put hundreds of hours in this game, and the amount of free content added to the game post-launch is mind-boggling.
